To bequeath something means to formally leave it to someone after you die, through a legal document called a will (also called a "last will and testament").

Think of it this way: Before a person dies, they can write a legal document saying, "After I'm gone, I want my house to go to my daughter, my savings to go to my son, and my old piano to go to my best friend." The act of formally deciding and declaring that — through a will — is called bequeathing.

So when someone dies and leaves their belongings to specific people through a will, they have bequeathed those things.

There are two sides to every act of bequeathing:

The person who bequeaths is usually called the testator — the one who writes the will and decides who gets what. This person must be alive when they write the will, but the actual transfer of belongings happens only after they pass away.

The person who receives what is bequeathed is called the beneficiary or heir. This can be a family member, a friend, an organization, a charity — anyone the testator chooses.

Almost anything of value that a person owns can be bequeathed:

  • Money — a sum from a bank account
  • Property — a house, land, or apartment
  • Personal items — jewelry, artwork, furniture, books, a musical instrument
  • Financial assets — stocks, bonds, investments
  • Intellectual property — the rights to a book, a song, or a patent

The key is that these things are transferred only after death, and only because the person formally documented their wishes in a will.
How It Is Used in Sentences

The most natural sentence pattern is: [Person] bequeathed [thing] to [someone].

  • "She bequeathed her entire art collection to the national museum."
  • "He bequeathed $200,000 to his nephew."
  • "The professor bequeathed all his research notes to the university."
  • "The estate was bequeathed to three different charities." (passive form)

You can also say it the other way around — [someone] was bequeathed [thing]:

  • "His granddaughter was bequeathed the family home."

When something is bequeathed, the thing that is left behind is called a bequest. So:

  • The act → to bequeath
  • The thing received → a bequest

"The library received a generous bequest from the late professor." means the professor bequeathed something (money or books, for example) to the library, and what the library received is called the bequest.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Give is broad and everyday — you can give someone a gift at any moment, while you're fully alive and present. Bequeath is specifically tied to death and a legal will.

Donate usually means giving to a cause or organization, often for charitable reasons, and almost always while you're still alive. You can donate to a charity today. Bequeathing happens only after death.

Leave (as in "leave something to someone") is the informal, everyday version of bequeath. People say "She left her house to her son" in normal conversation, while "She bequeathed her house to her son" is the more precise, formal way to say it — and carries the clear implication that a legal will was involved.
The Figurative Use — and This Is Important

Bequeath is also used in a broader, non-legal sense to describe passing something meaningful — not just physical property — from one generation to another, or from one person/group to the next. This is very common in writing and speeches.

In this sense, the "thing bequeathed" is often something abstract: values, traditions, knowledge, problems, opportunities, a legacy.

Examples:

  • "Every generation bequeaths its unresolved problems to the next."
  • "The great teacher bequeathed a love of literature to all her students."
  • "We must not bequeath a damaged environment to our children."
  • "The founder bequeathed the company a culture of innovation that lasted for decades."

In all these cases, nothing is being written in a legal will. But the word bequeath is used because something deeply meaningful is being passed on — almost as a gift — from someone (or a generation) to someone else who comes after them. The word carries a sense of gravity, of permanence, and of intentional passing-on. That's why writers and speakers choose it over simpler words like "give" or "pass on" when they want to emphasize the weight and significance of what is being transferred.

This is worth understanding. Bequeath is not a casual word. It carries a sense of solemnity, intention, and lasting significance. When you use it — even in its figurative sense — it signals that what is being passed on is not trivial. It matters. It is meant to endure. That emotional weight is part of what makes this word distinct and powerful.

What it meansTo formally leave something to someone after you die, through a will
Who does itThe testator (the person who writes the will)
Who receives itThe beneficiary or heir
When it happensAfter the testator's death
The related nounBequest (the thing that is bequeathed)
Figurative usePassing something meaningful — values, problems, a legacy — to the next generation or person
Tone of the wordFormal, solemn, weighty

Bequeath is the word for the act of making sure that something you value — whether a diamond ring or a set of beliefs — finds its way to the right hands after you are gone.
